transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2028-02-08 08:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (LumenHealth Head ML), Daniel Wu (LumenHealth Platform), Priya Rao (LumenHealth SRE), Alex Kline (Product)
Agenda: quick results recap, TTFT and streaming tuning, sequence-length hedging, kernel choices, next steps and handoff
Links shared: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/lumen-2028-02 (benchmark CSV), drive:sheet://lumen/pilot-notes (pilot notes), deck: https://redwood.app/decks/lumen-pilot-feb8.pdf

Summary (auto):
- Short recap of last week's microburst hit in first-token path; DEEP dive into kernel choices for 2k and 8k seqlen; tradeoffs between continuous batching vs aggressive prefix caching discussed.
- Agreed to run two kernel variants in parallel for 72h with sampled traffic; Redwood to deliver trimmed CSV and config protos.
- Customer to provide microburst traces and open platform access for remote profiling.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right hi everyone thanks for joining, um we have about 40 minutes so we'll try to keep it tight. Ethan and Lina will drive the tech bits. Sofia, Priya thanks for making time.
[00:12] Sofia Martinez: Yeah thanks Maya, been a busy week but keen to see the numbers, we had that micro burst on thursday and it shook our tail latency.
[00:18] Ethan Park: hey, rough one. We pulled the traces, and the first token path is where we saw the variance, the rest of the stream is more stable. We're gonna go through the TTFT numbers now.
[00:29] Daniel Wu: quick note — our infra team pushed a config change for the pod autoscaler yesterday, wonder if that affected queued requests.
[00:36] Lina Gomez: might show up in the queuing, yep. We flagged that in the raw logs.
[00:41] Maya Chen: ok 1st slide is trimmed: median TTFT down to 85ms on the new short-kernel but the 95/99 show spikes to 420ms. CSV link in chat.
[01:02] Priya Rao: those 420s line up with times we saw bursts of 30 concurrent small requests, like real-time tokenization calls from the front end.
[01:16] Ethan Park: exactly — looks like microbursts saturate the continuous batcher and we fall back to the wide kernel which has higher setup cost. Our idea: maintain a light-weight short-path kernel for first 1-2 tokens, then switch to heavy kernel for long outputs.
[01:36] Alex Kline: is that switching expensive in terms of KV cache or state?
[01:40] Ethan Park: a little; we have to stitch the KV cache pointers but it's constant-time if we keep the same shard, it's more overhead if we cross-device. In practice we've seen ~2-4ms penalty switching kernels, not the hundreds.
[01:59] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[02:05] Sofia Martinez: can you explain the 'short-kernel' and 'wide-kernel' naming — some of our infra folks misread it in the doc as 'short-curl' so just wanted clarity.
[02:14] Ethan Park: yeah fair, short-kernel = small sequence-optimized kernels with minimal startup, usually best for TTFT; wide-kernel = throughput-optimized, good for long sequences 2k+.
[02:29] Lina Gomez: note, quantization differences can change the perf shape; 4-bit fastquant tends to widen the 95th a bit.
[02:36] Daniel Wu: are we on quantized bits in the pilot? we left the model at 8-bit for quality right now.
[02:41] Ethan Park: correct, Lumen is on 8-bit plus some kernel-specific fusions. We suggested testing 4-bit fastquant for non-critical paths to save burst capacity.
[02:51] Maya Chen: next up streaming — we saw that streaming handshake added about 12ms median but stable; however when microbursts overlap with KV cache miss the streaming path stalls.
[03:08] Priya Rao: that matches our dashboard — we get a small bump for steady state but the real issue is the cache miss windows.
[03:18] Ethan Park: Right. Two levers: more aggressive prefix/KV caching and prefer-short-path hedging. Aggressive caching lowers token compute but increases memory. Tradeoff call for SRE.
[03:34] Sofia Martinez: memory footprint is okay but we have strict limits on host-side memory per pod — can't double it.
[03:41] Ethan Park: understood, so we propose adaptive caching: keep 128 tokens cached per session, but for sessions with high concurrency we pin only common prefixes. We'll include a policy sample.
[03:57] Alex Kline: about routing — can we route small requests to a dedicated pool?
[04:04] Lina Gomez: yes, Redwood routing rules support size-based routing; you can route by token-budget header. But that costs pool reservation.
[04:12] Daniel Wu: cost is a concern — team asked about price delta.
[04:16] Maya Chen: we'll put a rough delta in the notes; expect reserved small-pool to be 1.2x on unit cost but reduce TTFT variance a lot for tiny requests.
[04:31] [06:00] (background chatter)
[04:40] Ethan Park: ok kernel choices: we shortlisted three candidates — K-A (ultra short start), K-B (balanced), K-C (throughput fuse). Running A/B across synthetic microburst and captured traces.
[04:54] Priya Rao: how do you pick when to switch between K-A and K-C mid-request?
[04:58] Ethan Park: heuristics: if predicted output length > 256 tokens we plan a switch at token 4; otherwise stay on K-A. Prediction is from prompt length + sampling temp. It's an estimate not perfect.
[05:14] Sofia Martinez: prediction errors worry us, because a wrong switch could force a re-encode.
[05:20] Lina Gomez: we don't re-encode — we stitch KV. Worst case is a 4–10ms stall, not full recompute.
[05:30] Maya Chen: quick detour — security ask: can you confirm SSO + SAML and KMS support for private deployment? Sofia?
[05:38] Sofia Martinez: yes that's a blocker for our legal but final signoff is fine if SOC2 + SSO + customer KMS.
[05:45] Maya Chen: Redwood supports SAML SSO, audit logs, and we can integrate customer KMS. We'll share compliance pack.
[05:52] Daniel Wu: audit log retention options? we need 2 years.
[05:56] Maya Chen: enterprise tier has configurable retention; we will include exact retention SLAs in the doc.
[06:03] Ethan Park: back to perf. We ran a 24h pilot with a 5% traffic shadow and saw K-A drops median TTFT from 120ms to 82ms, but 99th stayed at ~390ms — those were the cross-device cases.
[06:22] Priya Rao: cross-device as in when the session moves across different GPU instances?
[06:26] Ethan Park: yep, when autoscaler rebalanced or during a scale-up event. We're recommending affinity pinning for short-path requests to reduce that.
[06:37] Alex Kline: affinity pinning means we risk uneven utilization.
[06:41] Lina Gomez: it's a knob — you can pin for a sliding window then release. That smooths variance without long term imbalance.
[06:52] Maya Chen: proposed experiment: 72h parallel run with two kernel configs: Config A = K-A short-path enabled + adaptive caching; Config B = K-B default with conservative caching. We'll run with 5% live traffic sampled and with replay of microburst traces.
[07:13] Sofia Martinez: timeline?
[07:16] Maya Chen: start 2028-02-11, run through 2028-02-14. Redwood to share final config and scripts by 2028-02-12.
[07:28] Daniel Wu: what metrics do you need? we can feed token-level latency, pod metrics, and histograms.
[07:35] Ethan Park: token-level TTFT histogram (per route), streaming latency, KV cache miss ratio, and pod-level GC/IO stats. A combined timeline is best.
[07:45] Priya Rao: we'll grant read-only access to our prometheus and upload microburst traces to the shared drive.
[07:52] Maya Chen: great. Also note — we recommended a small change to your NLB idle timeout to avoid mid-stream connection resets; Daniel, can you follow up with infra?
[07:58] Daniel Wu: yeah will do, I'll flag in ticket #4522.
[08:04] Speaker 4: (crosstalk)
[08:08] Lina Gomez: one more detail on quantization: in our bench, 4-bit with the new kernel fusion reduces median by ~20% but increases variance a bit on 95th under microbursts. So lean to keep 8-bit for streaming critical paths.
[08:27] Maya Chen: so action items recap in chat now. Anything else?
[08:33] Alex Kline: curious about fallback policy — if the short-path fails, do we fallback to CPU?
[08:38] Ethan Park: fallback policy is model-variant fallback on GPU pools, not CPU; we avoid CPU fallback due to latency. We may spill to a lower-capacity GPU pool with slightly higher latency but preserved availability.
[08:49] Sofia Martinez: that's preferable. CPU fallback would kill SLA.
[08:53] Maya Chen: okay closing with handoff notes — Redwood will hand off configs, perf scripts, and a short runbook for on-call to Priya. We'll sync after the 72h experiment for result triage.
[09:07] Priya Rao: sounds good, we'll schedule a 30-minute triage on 2028-02-15.
[09:12] Maya Chen: perfect, thanks everyone.
[09:15] [END]
notes: Experiment: 72h parallel run (2028-02-11 to 2028-02-14) with K-A vs K-B; Redwood to provide configs and perf scripts; Lumen to provide microburst traces and infra access. Compliance pack + retention details to be shared.
